title: The Buyer Type You Attract Decides the Price You Get
excerpt: The same business can be worth three different numbers depending on who is buying it. A trade buyer, a private equity fund and your own management team are never pricing the same thing.
content:
Owners tend to talk about their business as if it has one true value, a single number sitting quietly in the background waiting to be confirmed by whoever eventually makes an offer. In practice, that number moves depending on who is doing the buying. A trade buyer, a private equity fund and the business's own management team are rarely pricing the same thing, even when they are looking at identical financials.

The pattern we see across owner-led businesses on the East Coast is that most exit planning starts with the financials and stops there, without asking who the likely buyer actually is. That question changes almost everything else, what gets prepared, what gets highlighted in the numbers, and realistically, what the business is worth to the person signing the cheque.

The Trade Buyer Is Paying for What They Would Otherwise Have to Build

A competitor or an adjacent business buying for strategic reasons is rarely just buying a profit line. They are buying a customer base they would otherwise spend years and real marketing budget acquiring, a team with skills they are currently short of, or simply one fewer competitor pushing on their pricing. That additional value, often called synergy value, sits on top of what the standalone financials would suggest, and it is the reason trade buyers can sometimes pay more than a purely financial return would justify.

The catch is that this premium is never automatic. It shows up only when the seller can clearly articulate what the buyer gains beyond the P&L, market access, a gap in their service line, geographic reach into Queensland or Victoria they do not currently have. Sellers who only present a set of accounts and wait for the buyer to work out the strategic case usually leave that premium on the table, because it is not the buyer's job to build the argument for paying more.

The Financial Buyer Is Paying for Certainty, Not a Growth Story

A private equity fund or other financial buyer is underwriting a return over a defined holding period, typically three to five years, and their price is built backwards from the multiple they expect to exit at, not forwards from how promising the story sounds today. What they reward is predictable, recurring cash flow, a management layer that does not depend entirely on the owner, and clean, defensible numbers that will not unravel under the due diligence a fund is contractually obliged to run.

This is where the same growth story that excites a trade buyer can actually work against a financial buyer, if that growth has come with thinner margins, customer concentration, or an owner who is still the person every major client calls first. Financial buyers discount hard for exactly the things an exit readiness diagnostic is designed to surface early, owner dependence, contract quality, customer concentration, so the gaps are closed on the seller's timeline rather than found and priced down on the buyer's.

The Management Buyout Rarely Gets Funded by the Business Being Sold

Selling to the existing management team is often the quietest, least disruptive exit available, and for the right business it protects culture and continuity in a way an external sale rarely can. It also tends to settle at a lower headline price than a trade or financial sale, mostly because of how it gets funded. A management team is usually borrowing against personal assets or relying on vendor finance, where the seller accepts part of the price over time, rather than drawing on the deep pockets an external buyer brings to the table.

None of that makes a management buyout the wrong choice, for many owner-led businesses it is the right one, but it does mean going in with a clear view of what the price will realistically look like and how the financing will actually work is worth doing early. A structured look at capital raise preparation before the conversation starts gives everyone a shared, realistic starting point instead of a number the management team can never actually finance.

Knowing Your Likely Buyer Changes What You Prepare For

None of this means an owner needs to pick a buyer type years in advance and prepare for nothing else. It means the preparation itself should not be generic. A business gearing up for a trade sale spends its energy building the strategic story a competitor would pay for. One heading toward a financial buyer spends it de-risking owner dependence and tightening the numbers. One considering a management buyout spends it structuring a financeable deal rather than chasing a headline figure nobody involved can actually pay.

Most owners only discover which buyer they have actually attracted once an approach lands, which is usually too late to change how the business has been prepared. An indicative business valuation run ahead of that moment gives a grounded starting figure across methodologies, and a conversation about which buyer type is realistically in reach for a business of this size and shape. That is a far steadier position to negotiate from than discovering, mid conversation, that the number in your head was built for a buyer who was never actually going to show up.

faqs.q: Do private equity buyers pay more or less than trade buyers?
faqs.a: It depends on the business, not a fixed rule. Trade buyers can pay a premium when there is clear synergy value, a customer base or market access they would otherwise have to build themselves. Financial buyers price off predictable cash flow and a defined return, so a business with thin margins or heavy owner dependence often gets a lower offer from a fund than from a competitor.

faqs.q: What is the difference between a trade buyer and a financial buyer?
faqs.a: A trade buyer is usually a competitor or adjacent business buying for strategic reasons, market access, customer base, removing a competitor, and can price in value beyond the standalone financials. A financial buyer, typically a private equity fund, is underwriting a return over a set holding period and prices almost entirely off predictable, defensible cash flow.

faqs.q: How does a management buyout affect the sale price of a business?
faqs.a: Management buyouts tend to settle at a lower headline price than external sales, mainly because of financing constraints. The buying team is usually borrowing against personal assets or relying on vendor finance rather than drawing on the capital an external buyer brings, which caps what they can realistically pay upfront. Reviewing capital raise preparation early sets a financeable expectation.

faqs.q: Why would a competitor pay more for my business than an investor?
faqs.a: A competitor can be buying more than the profit line, a customer base, a team, or a gap in their own service offering they would otherwise spend years building. That additional value sits on top of the standalone financials. An investor is pricing a return on capital, so unless that strategic story is made explicit, a competitor's offer can land meaningfully higher.

faqs.q: Can I sell my business to my management team without external finance?
faqs.a: Often yes, though it usually involves some combination of the team's own borrowing capacity and vendor finance, where the seller accepts part of the price over time rather than all of it at settlement. It is worth structuring this deliberately rather than assuming the headline price of an external sale simply transfers across to an internal one.

faqs.q: How do I know what type of buyer my business will attract?
faqs.a: It comes down to size, margin structure, owner dependence and how replicable the customer relationships are. An exit readiness diagnostic scores the business across the dimensions each buyer type cares about most, which gives a realistic read on who is actually likely to be interested, rather than who the owner assumes will be.

faqs.q: Is an indicative business valuation useful before I know who the buyer will be?
faqs.a: Yes, and arguably more useful before that point than after. An indicative business valuation gives a defensible figure across methodologies and flags the value drivers and detractors that will matter regardless of buyer type, so the owner is negotiating from grounded numbers rather than a guess that only holds up for one kind of buyer.
